name: Mpur
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Mpur (mpur1239) is not in the catalog. Both sweep items are by Cecilia Odé: the 2002 ELPR monograph 'Mpur prosody' (print only, no digital copy anywhere I could reach: no HathiTrust record, Google Books no-preview, not in UvA-DARE, ELPR host dead) and the 2000 Rodopi/Brill six-page contact note (paywalled DOI 10.1163/9789004488472_028; archive.org lending scan restricted). Neither could be read. Instead the sweep obtained two open first-hand Odé texts: her 2002 'A sketch of Mpur' in Pacific Linguistics 524 (sealang CC BY-SA PDF, text layer) whose sec. 2.4 Stress (p. 51) states there is no evidence that lexical stress is phonologically significant, no regular prominence pattern exists, and the same word shifts prominence across contexts; and her 1997 Eurospeech paper (ISCA open PDF, scanned) p. 183: 'There is no evidence for phonemic lexical stress in Mpur.' Mpur is a lexical tone language (three tones H/M/L in the sketch; five perceptual contrasts in 1997; Remijsen 2001/2007 on file cite 3-5 / 4 tones). Reesink's volume overview (sec. 7.1, printed p. 26 = PDF p. 36; the catalog's Meyah record mislocates this as p. 22) confirms 'Mpur clearly has phonemic tone'. Recommended new record: no word stress / tone language, deciding source Odé 2002 sketch sec. 2.4. Remaining acquisition wants: Odé 2002 monograph (medium; would settle tone count and upgrade evidence grade) and Kalmbacher 1996 SIL 'Mpur phonology' MS (medium; Odé says it disagrees on word stress and tone). searches were done via Glottolog, Crossref, archive.org, Google Books feed API, ISCA archive, UvA-DARE and curl.

new_statements.quote: In polysyllabic words, a syllable can be more prominent than its surrounding syllables, especially if it has high tone or a relatively longer duration. Yet there is no evidence that lexical stress in Mpur is phonologically significant. In a pilot experiment conducted in the field, I observed that no regular pattern of realised prominence of syllables exists. In different contexts one and the same word may even show shifting prominence without expressing a contrast.
new_statements.citation: Odé, Cecilia. 2002. A sketch of Mpur. In Ger P. Reesink (ed.), Languages of the eastern Bird's Head (Pacific Linguistics 524), 45-107. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-524.45
new_statements.locator: §2.4 Stress, p. 51 (PDF page 61 of PL-524); see also §2 Phonology p. 48 and §2.3 Tones pp. 50-51
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mpur is a lexical-tone language (three attested level tones H/M/L, possibly a fourth mid-rising; Odé 1997 works with five perceptual contrasts). There is no phonologically significant word stress: syllable prominence in polysyllabic words is a by-product of high tone or longer duration, shows no regular position, and shifts for the same word across contexts without contrast. Corroborated first-hand by Odé 1997:183: 'There is no evidence for phonemic lexical stress in Mpur.'
new_statements.exceptions: None. Odé notes (p. 48) that Kalmbacher's unpublished 1996 phonology differs from hers 'especially... with respect to word stress and the tone system', without saying how.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (polysyllabic words, in context); based on a field pilot experiment plus instrumental stylization of recordings from 18 speakers of several dialects. Phrase-level prominence is handled by intonation (§2.5): large pitch movements and final-syllable lengthening at prosodic boundaries, focus marker ni, enclitics and word repetition.
new_statements.identity_note: Odé's sketch covers Mpur as a whole (Kebar, Amberbaken and Arfu dialects; fieldwork at Anjai/Kebar and Saukorem/Amberbaken with speakers of all three, 1993-95); she reports only that 'there are some dialectal differences' in tone. Miedema & Welling 1985 call the language Amberbaken with dialects Kebar, Amberbaken and Arfu (Kebar+Arfu = Pur). No separate glottocodes.

new_statements.citation: Odé, Cecilia (2002). A sketch of Mpur. In Ger P. Reesink (ed.), Languages of the eastern Bird's Head, 45-108. Pacific Linguistics 524. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-524.45.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.4 Stress, p. 51 (PDF p. 61 of PL-524); cf. sec. 2 preamble p. 48 and sec. 2.3 Tones pp. 50-51
new_statements.reading: Mpur has no phonologically significant word stress and no fixed or predictable prominence position; it is a lexical tone language (three tones H/M/L per this sketch, with a possible fourth tone unresolved; 1997 paper counted five perceptual contrasts). Any catalog record should be coded as a no-word-stress / tone language, not as fixed or weight-sensitive stress. Corroborated first-hand by Odé 1997 Eurospeech p. 183 ('There is no evidence for phonemic lexical stress in Mpur') and second-hand by Reesink 2002 p. 26 ('Mpur clearly has phonemic tone'). Caveat: Kalmbacher's unpublished 1996 SIL phonology is said by Odé to differ on word stress and tone.

sources.quote: Mpur clearly has phonemic tone, Meyah and Sougb a pitch-accent system. Hatam and Mansim do not have a tonal distinction, which they may well have had in the past (the number of homophones in Hatam is considerable), but Hatam does have a very pronounced iambic stress pattern over the utterance as a whole, defying attempts to determine a pattern of word stress.
sources.locator: sec. 7.1 Phonology, p. 26 (PDF p. 36) — NB the catalog's Meyah (meya1236) record cites this passage as 'p. 22'; the printed page is 26
sources.note: Comparative remark only: 'Mpur clearly has phonemic tone, Meyah and Sougb a pitch-accent system'; the iambic utterance-level stress remark concerns Hatam, not Mpur.

sources.citation: Odé, Cecilia (1997). A descriptive study of prosodic phenomena in Mpur (West Papuan Phylum). Proc. Eurospeech 1997 (Rhodes), vol. 1, 183-186. DOI 10.21437/Eurospeech.1997-73.
sources.quote: On the basis of production and perception data, analysed by means of the perceptual analysis-by-resynthesis method for the stylization of pitch phenomena [3], a classification into five perceptual lexical tone contrasts has been arrived at: four level tones (high, mid (unmarked), midlow and low) and one contour tone (falling&rising) (henceforth H, M, ML, L, FR, respectively) [4], [5]; there are some dialectal differences. There is no evidence for phonemic lexical stress in Mpur.
sources.note: Independent earlier first-hand statement by the same fieldworker (18 speakers, recordings 1993-95): no evidence for phonemic lexical stress; Mpur is a tone language (here five perceptual tone contrasts, later reduced to three phonological tones in the 2002 sketch). Paper itself is about boundary tone realisation, vowel lengthening and emphatic repetition, not stress placement.
